Why is today's AI chip competition
different from any previous computer revolution?
The answer is not just computing power.
Dave Patterson started by posing the most crucial question of the day:
Why is today a silicon gold mine? What are the essential differences between
it and the Lisp machine craze of the 1980s and the supercomputer wave of the 1990s
Bill Daly's answer was direct.
He believes that what truly defines this round of AI revolution
are three conditions that have never appeared simultaneously before:
real business demand, a unified computing paradigm,
and a software ecosystem with virtually no historical baggage.
Many golden ages of computer architecture in the past were
heavily influenced by scientific research. The
development of supercomputers in the 1990s
largely relied on funding from government projects like DARPA, leading to the
birth of numerous startups. However,
very few of these startups managed to establish a sustainable commercial market. Even
star companies like Thinking Machines eventually failed.
Therefore, technological leadership alone
cannot sustain an industry.
AI is completely different.
Today, almost every industry is trying to incorporate AI into its business,
from search and programming to healthcare and manufacturing. The
market demand for tokens, computing power, and inference capabilities is
growing almost infinitely. The
driving force behind chip innovation is no longer subsidies,
but customers who are truly willing to pay continuously.
This is why this wave can go further.
Here's a counterintuitive point:
Bill Daly said that
Transformers are actually a relatively simple application.
This statement might seem contradictory at first glance, given that
large models have trillions of parameters and
training costs are higher than any previous computational task.
However, he emphasized that by "simple," he meant the
computational structure, not the model size.
In the past, high-performance computing,
such as weather simulation, fluid dynamics, and kernel computing,
often involved hundreds of thousands or even millions of lines of code.
Even if you speed up the most time-consuming computing cores tenfold, the
real bottleneck is still that huge amount of sequential code.
This is the reason why Amdahl's Law has long limited the development of supercomputing.
Transformers are different.
Their computation is highly concentrated on a few core operators such as matrix multiplication, attention, softmax, and layernorm.
For hardware architects,
as long as they continuously optimize around these core primitives, the
entire model can simultaneously achieve huge improvements. This is
why GPUs and TPUs can evolve at a much faster speed than traditional CPUs.
Previously, they had to support thousands of applications;
now, they have to continuously refine a limited number of computing modes. For the
first time, hardware and models have formed a highly consistent direction of evolution.
Transformers have changed not only AI but
also the methodology of chip design.

biggest difficulty in the software ecosystem is often not performance

AI hardly has this problem.
